text: Joseph had been taken down to Egypt, and Potiphar, an Egyptian officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him there.

versions.text: Joseph had been taken down to Egypt, and Potiphar, an Egyptian who was one of Pharaoh's officials, the captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him there.
versions.explanation: For oral reading, the stacked appositives ("an Egyptian who was one of Pharaoh's officials, the captain of the guard") make the subject hard to track before the verb arrives. Tightening the titles keeps the same information with a smoother spoken rhythm.

text: The LORD was with Joseph, and he prospered. He lived in the house of his Egyptian master,
and his master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD gave success to everything he did.
So Joseph found favor in his eyes and became his personal attendant. He put him in charge of his household and entrusted everything he owned to his care.

From the time he put Joseph in charge of his house and all he owned, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's household because of Joseph. The blessing of the LORD rested on everything he had, both in the house and in the field.
So he left everything he owned in Joseph's care and gave no thought to anything except the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome and well built.
After some time, his master's wife took notice of Joseph and said, "Come to bed with me."
But he refused. "Look," he said to her, "my master gives no thought to anything in this house; he has put everything he owns into my hands.
No one in this house stands above me, and he has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. How then could I do such a great evil and sin against God?"
Day after day she kept at him, but he would not listen to her or lie with her or be with her.
One such day he came into the house to do his work, and none of the household servants was there.
She caught hold of his cloak and said, "Come to bed with me!" But he left his cloak in her hand and ran out of the house.
When she saw that he had left his cloak in her hand and had fled outside,

she called the men of her household and said to them, "Look, he has brought us a Hebrew to make sport of us! He came to me to lie with me, but I screamed at the top of my voice." [Footnote: "He" here refers to her husband, the master of the house — an accusation she repeats in verse 17.]

versions.text: she called the household servants and said to them, "Look, this Hebrew was brought to us to make sport of us! He came to me to lie with me, but I screamed at the top of my voice.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb הֵבִיא is active with an unnamed subject (her husband), and the accusatory jab at her husband is part of the rhetoric, echoed in v. 17 ("that Hebrew slave you brought us"). The passive "was brought to us" loses that pointed accusation and breaks the link with v. 17.

versions.text: she called the household servants and said to them, "Look, he has brought us a Hebrew to make sport of us! He came to me to lie with me, but I screamed at the top of my voice.
versions.explanation: Two small points. (1) Since verse 13 ends with "he had fled outside" (Joseph), the unmarked "he has brought us" can momentarily be misheard as still referring to Joseph; a brief footnote identifying the subject as her husband preserves the pointed accusation (kept from the earlier revision) without altering the text. (2) אַנְשֵׁי בֵיתָהּ is literally "the men of her household," which is significant here since she is deliberately summoning male witnesses; "the men of her household" is both more accurate and reads smoothly aloud.

text: When he heard me raise my voice and scream, he left his cloak beside me and ran out of the house."
She kept his cloak beside her until his master came home,
and then she told him the same story: "That Hebrew slave you brought us came to me to make sport of me.
But when I raised my voice and screamed, he left his cloak beside me and fled outside."
When his master heard what his wife told him—"This is how your slave treated me"—he burned with anger.
Joseph's master took him and put him in the prison where the king's prisoners were held, and there he remained.
But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love, and he granted him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.
The warden put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners in the prison, and everything that was done there was done by him.
The warden paid no attention to anything under Joseph's care, because the LORD was with him and gave him success in whatever he did.
